newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solvay says yr to April net up slightly.
newsitem.headline: Solvay says yr to April net up slightly.

text.p: Net earnings at Belgian chemicals and drugs group Solvay in the first four months of 1997 were slightly better than those for the same period of 1996, chief executive officer Daniel Janssen told the annual general meeting on Thursday.
He gave no profit figure, adding, "It is difficult to give a 12-month forecast because we are living in a world in which changes are many and rapid."

Solvay had 1996 consolidated net profit of 13.63 billion francs, up from 12.51 billion in 1995. Without a 2.09 billion franc extraordinary gain, net current profit was 11.54 billion, down from 12.54 billion.
In February Janssen said he was hoping that 1997 current profits would return to the 1995 level.

Hopes for 1997 were in part centred on an expected continuation of a recovery for PVC and high-density poly-ethylene prices, he said at the time. Together with polypropylene the two products make up the plastics sector, where results dropped by more than 50 percent in 1996.

Janssen told shareholders PVC selling prices continued to increase in the first few months of 1997, but they were still not high enough to cover ethylene price increases and restore the European PVC activities to satisfactory profitability.
Cost cutting at the European PVC units continued.
Volume growth was more favourable in Asia and in Latin America, he added.
Sustained by strong demand, high-density polyethylene was improving. "Overall 1997 should be a better year for plastics than 1996," Janssen said.

In alkalis caustic soda prices began to trend up in June. Other activities continued to do well. In the first few months of 1997 sales of soda ash eased slightly in Europe while exports of natural ash to Asia and Latin America continued to increase.

An increase in income from peroxygens reversed in 1997. Pressure on prices worsened, especially in Europe, as the hydrogen-peroxide market stagnated, hit by the paper industry crisis. New capacity could not be absorbed.
Janssen said that here too Solvay was cutting costs. It had decided to postpone by six months the start-up of the 85,000 tonne hydrogen peroxide expansion in Deer Park, Texas.
Persalts were suffering from strong competition, leading to inadequate prices.

In processing, industrial sheets and films were benefitting from various restructurings. Decorative products were affected by stagnation in private consumption in Europe. Pipes and fittings were going well.
In pharmaceuticals sales continued to increase. In Europe rising pressure to control health costs put pressure on prices.
Janssen said Solvay would change the name of the Health Sector to the Pharmaceuticals Sector.
